sections.html:
• Common names: Dwarf Texan Crayfish
  • Scientific name: Cambarellus texanus
  • Optimal tank size: 40 litres
  • Breeding: easy
  • Optimal KH: 3–15
  • Optimal TDS: 200–300 (100–500)
  • Nitrate: less than 20 ppm
  • Diet: detritivore / omnivore
  • Temperament: conditionally peaceful
  • Colour: olive to brown with darkish stripes

According to the latest research, there are 19 species in the genus Cambarellus. They are all small (3–5 cm long) and look very similar apart from variation in colour and pattern, so they are hard to tell apart. On the market we can find, for example: Cambarellus ninae (brown), Cambarellus montezumae (yellow), Cambarellus patzcuarensis (orange), Cambarellus shufeldtii (grey/reddish to brown), Cambarellus texanus (olive to brown), Cambarellus diminutus (grey/reddish to brown or blue) and Cambarellus puer (orange-red to light brown).

This method of identification is not completely accurate and in some cases is totally compromised, because these dwarf crayfish can crossbreed, creating new colour variations and patterns. Basically, nobody can be absolutely sure which species they have.

This is a freshwater crayfish native to Texas. It was first found in a ditch near Bay City in Matagorda County, Texas. It has since been found in the Colorado River, Fort Bend County and Waller County.
Brazos Dwarf Crayfish inhabit ditches with standing water and lots of plants, and will burrow when the habitat becomes dry.

The bigger the tank, the better, as it can be set up with diverse areas for them to dwell in. Optimal tank size is about 40 litres.

They are great escape artists and will climb air hoses and silicone sealant, so a fitted lid should be placed on the tank. The water line should not be too high.

Brazos Dwarf Crayfish are usually straightforward and easy to care for. Although they are very hardy, there is no reason to test their limits: if the tank is not cycled, do not add the crayfish to cycle it. High ammonia and nitrate can still harm them.

Regular water changes are vital to their health. Proper filtration along with water changes keeps the crayfish properly oxygenated. Acclimating them is advisable despite their hardiness.

Brazos Dwarf Crayfish can safely be kept with any type of live plant. They do not eat healthy plants and benefit from plants by collecting bacteria and microorganisms off them.

Moulting: like all crustaceans, they must shed their exoskeleton to grow and to regrow lost limbs. An adult only needs to moult up to five times a year, whereas a juvenile moults every 7 to 10 days. While moulting they look for a place to hide, as they are defenceless until the exoskeleton fully hardens. Driftwood, rocks and plants are therefore crucial, otherwise they can fall prey to other crayfish or even to dwarf shrimp.

Temperature: in nature they live in a wide range of temperatures, 4–32°C. In the aquarium the optimal temperature is 18–24°C. They do not require a heater; room temperature suits them fine.

pH: although they come from areas with a high pH, they can also tolerate a low pH (6.5). The optimal pH is 7.0–8.0.

Hardness: optimal KH 3–15 and GH 3–18.

RO/DI water remineralised with Salty Shrimp GH/KH+ is recommended, though they can be kept in tap water, which is not the best option.

Sponge filters are the best option because of their surface area. Matten filters are highly recommended for any dwarf crayfish or shrimp tank, as dwarf crayfish will not damage and tear apart the sponge as large crayfish species often do.

If you use a canister or hang-on-back filter and plan to breed them, the filter intake should be covered with a sponge or net, because the babies are very tiny (about 2 mm) and can easily be sucked up.

Provide a sand or gravel substrate into which they can burrow. They can slightly change colour in response to their background to camouflage against predators. There should be plenty of dark hiding places made of rocks, driftwood, PVC pipe, plants and so on. If several are kept together, each needs its own hiding place in different parts of the tank, since they are territorial and do not like neighbours.

They will rearrange the tank over time, digging into the substrate and dragging anything light enough for them to move.

Brazos Dwarf Crayfish almost always spend their time scavenging for food. They are omnivores and prefer organic food. Suggested foods: blackworms, crushed snails, earthworms, brine shrimp, dead fish or shrimp. Algae wafers are a special treat.

They will eat basically anything put in the tank. Feed bottom-dwelling live food along with sinking pellets: shrimp pellets, shrimp granules, fish food (TetraMin flakes etc.), shrimp food (such as Hikari crustacean food, algae wafers) and frozen bloodworms. They also enjoy vegetables such as shelled peas and zucchini.

Supplement the diet with specialised invertebrate foods so they get enough calcium for the exoskeleton.

Snails and meaty foods are preferred and help them grow much faster. Algae wafers and vegetables should only be supplementary; the main diet should be meat (protein). Colour-enhancing food can help maintain or improve bright orange colouration.

How often: feed too much and you risk fouling the water and causing problems (black beard algae, hydras, planaria and so on); feed too little and the crayfish may go after shrimp or fish. Start with 3–4 times a week and adjust to your livestock's requirements.

Brazos Dwarf Crayfish are one of the few crayfish that can be kept in captivity relatively safely. They are less aggressive than larger crayfish (Blue, Red, Marbled, Cherax destructor and so on), but not completely peaceful.

Despite their small size they are quite territorial (especially males), defending their homes and threatening and fighting each other if they come too close. Some fights end badly for one of them, so they prefer to keep a distance from their own kind. If the tank is overpopulated they will regulate numbers in their own way, and you may see one or two lose a leg or claw, which grows back.

They are good diggers and often build burrows; in nature they burrow when habitats become too dry or too cold. They are mostly nocturnal.

Tankmates: they are not social and prefer to be alone in a community tank. They tend to react defensively, even running at you with raised claws.

Fish: no aggressive fish should be kept with them. If they feel threatened they may behave aggressively towards fish and take chunks out of fins, although they cannot kill most fish. They are often kept with small peaceful fish such as guppies, mollies and dwarf swordtails. Only ill and weak specimens can be caught.

Shrimp: results vary by individual. Some keepers manage to keep them with dwarf shrimp, while others blame them for a drastic reduction of the colony. Shrimp are not too fast for them. Keeping even dwarf crayfish with small shrimp is not recommended, except perhaps ghost shrimp, Amano shrimp, bamboo shrimp and vampire shrimp, which can grow bigger than the crayfish. Any moulting shrimp is an easy meal, and even baby crayfish can try to catch baby shrimp. Keeping them well fed reduces their hunting instinct.

Snails: they will try to catch small snails without an operculum, such as bladder (pest) snails. Large snails are usually safe, though the crayfish may nip off antennae now and then.

Bad tankmates: larger or aggressive fish, any other crayfish species, other freshwater crabs, dwarf frogs.

The sexes can be told apart externally by looking at the lower part of the abdomen. Males have an extra set of pleopods used for internal fertilisation, forming a triangular arrangement of small legs. Females have a seminal receptacle and lack these extra pleopods behind the walking legs; instead there is a small nub.

It is easy to tell them apart once they reach about 1.5 cm, at about 2 months old. Females are a little bigger than males and have a wider abdomen.

Breeding is considered easy and needs little intervention. Make sure there is at least one male and one female. They mature at about 2.5–3 months old.

If a female is ready to mate she allows a male to approach; the male clamps her claws and puts her on her back. Mating can last from several minutes to an hour or so. The female then folds her tail under her body to fertilise her eggs.

Females usually carry 10 to 50 eggs, and big females sometimes more. She keeps them clean and well oxygenated with her appendages. Hatching takes 3–4 weeks depending on temperature. Dark spots (developing eyes) on the eggs mean they are about to hatch.

After hatching, the young ride on the mother's back and under her tail for a couple of days, sometimes a week or two. They can only wiggle at this stage. Then they detach and crawl away. Maternal pheromones encourage the young to stay close and the female to protect them. Once these wear off, the young are better off far from their mother, so ideally isolate them in a rearing tank from the start, otherwise there is a great risk of her attacking and eating them.

Do not keep different generations together. Babies are also very aggressive, especially larger ones towards smaller ones, and even with a small size difference they will catch and kill smaller ones. Only babies of similar size can be kept together relatively safely.

Feed the babies daily in the early stages, otherwise they will die from hunger or aggression; being well fed decreases aggression. Once they are about 1.5–2 cm long, they can be placed with the adults, when it should be relatively safe.

Description: it reaches a maximum of 3 cm; carapace length is usually 8–12 mm. It has many curved, wave-like and dotted lines. The abdomen has a pale olive ground colour with a middorsal stripe lighter than the ground colour, outlined by dense stippling. A clearly visible dark spot is located in the centre of the tail. The body is covered with tiny dots with many pattern and colour variations. The pincers are elongated and narrow.

Lifespan is about 1.5–2 years, though some live a little longer under optimal conditions.
